body: Each item in this list is one paragraph. Write what you tried, what broke, and what you changed.
Add or remove paragraphs as you like. Each one is wrapped in "straight quotes" and separated by commas.

Enrico taped out the field dimensions on the classroom floor and started driving Buzz around to see how he handles. He found the wheels have to be kept really clean or the robot doesn't move the way it should. A fine toothbrush gets the dirt out.
We also got a Mac set up for the team this week, and moved the laser cutter and the 3D printers to a spot in my classroom where they can stay put.
caption: The laser cutter in its new spot, vented and working.

body: Ethan and Myles officially got the laser cutter to work and mastered the way you're supposed to use it. Jack worked on a makeshift new piece of a robot idea, which could help us with Buzz, while Athena did the same, but with the VEX IQ parts.
Next we will organize our tools, and 3D print some field elements.
caption: Athena prototyping an arm out of VEX IQ parts.

body: Myles actually learned to code the robot to go through the obstacle course, and boosted its mechanics to go at a speed it can't go higher. He and Enrico got the robot through the course to test its intelligence and response to our codes.
Nathan was working on a makeshift scissor lift. If it works, it may be very useful if the challenge involves altitude.
caption: Writing the code to get Buzz through the course.

body: Half day, so no meeting. Here's most of the team anyway.
This was the first day we had our robot ready! After mastering how to control it, we were basically playing around with the robot and testing out its new movements.

Myles and Enrico were testing out the new robot and getting the hang of its remote control, Athena was working on the bingo night presentation and fundraiser, and Nathan was working on some extra creative robot parts. In the other room, Ethan worked on the online challenges and ideas for the website.
We also coded on a soundboard for fun!
This day was packed, a lot of things were going down simultaneously. We also figured out a name for the robot. Buzz McTwinkletoes! We'll call him Buzz.
caption: Buzz on the move, the first day he was ready to drive.

body: The name might not stick. They're still going back and forth on it.

We had our VEX IQ robot parts delivered! Ethan started building the robot and learning its design model, while Athena and Enrico were planning out expenses for bingo night, and Myles was getting the new motor to work.
Overall, we made tons of progress that day.
caption: The VEX IQ kit open on the floor the day it came in.

body: We started to plan out our materials and expenses online for bingo night. We also started making some prototypes that we could possibly add to our robot.
Towards the end of the day, we planned out our preview files for the online challenges.
Calibrated both 3D printers and ran a test print.
caption: First test run after calibrating.

body: We got to know how the tournament will work and a preview of what we will be getting into.
We checked out the kit of the robot parts, and we started to sculpt some ideas on CAD.
caption: Working out a game idea on the board.

body: Two students who are both completely new to this worked out two different problems in the same meeting, sitting next to each other.

The first one couldn't get the one meter challenge to land. He found rotation numbers for the LEGO wheels online and they weren't getting him close. So he stopped using rotations. He timed how long the robot took to cross a meter and programmed it to drive for that many seconds instead. It worked. Timing drifts as a battery drains so we won't use it on the competition robot, but it got him there.

The other one's robot kept curving instead of driving straight. His two motors were starting one after the other in the same stack, so one had a head start. He added a second "when program starts" block and ran each motor from its own, and it went straight.
We're keeping the name Mighty Bees and we'll ask for last year's team number if nobody has taken it. A few people want to put together a segment for the morning show.
caption: The one-metre drive, finally landing on the mark.

body: The 3D printers are leaving thin strings of plastic across everything they print. We think something changed in the software over the summer rather than the machines being broken, but we haven't proved it.

We want to enter the online challenge where you design a game in CAD: https://recf.org/online_challenge/no-title-2/. It's something the whole team can work on and it doesn't need the robot. We can't sign up for it until the team itself is registered, and we're hoping to get that done Monday.
Spent the rest of the time on team roles, the website, and ideas for raising money.
New challenge. Build an arm that picks a tennis ball up off the floor and holds it above the hub.
Almost every first attempt stalled. The arms were long and the motors couldn't turn them with the ball out at the end. One group shortened theirs. Another geared it down and kept the length.
I'm staying hands off on purpose right now. They're coming up with their own ideas and working through the problems themselves, which is what the engineering is.
caption: Three arms going at once.

body: First real challenge. Build something that drives exactly one meter and stops. Not close to a meter. Measured with a tape measure on the floor.

Nobody got it on the first try. Most were off by 10 or 15 centimeters. The students who did FIRST LEGO League last year knew to go look up the wheel size first. The newer ones started by guessing and adjusting.
We opened the bins and told everyone to build something that moves. No challenge, no rules.
Some of the group did FIRST LEGO League last year and went straight to work. A couple have never touched any of this. By five there were several things driving around on the floor.
caption: The first day's builds.
